Lesson 1.
Don't treat bike routes like highways.
When I biked the heavily traveled cycling route from Amsterdam to Harlem, I expected
it to be off-street bike trail the entire way.
After all, this country could make it happen.
But instead, it features six different types of bike infrastructure, some of which is
actually shared with cars.
But the important part is that safety is continuous, with the route adapting to the environments
it travels through.
Compare that to how Radner Township PA is handling their portion of the circuit, a partially
completed network of bike trails connecting the Philly region.
Their job is to connect the existing Radner Trail to the Norristown High Speed Line, where
it will follow the tracks to Southwest Philly.

thousand feet under the highway, build some crossings in Voila.

on cheap, easy, and practical connections first, because there's no Robert Moses for

Lesson 2, Know What Not To Build.
When people talk about bike protection, they often describe it as an accessory for after
a city finishes attending to the needs of cars.
This idea, besides being just plain evil, contains an unspoken assumption that streets are
dangerous to cyclists by default.
Quite the opposite.
The world's roads and streets used to be pretty safe for cycling, because cars were not

youtube_description: This summer, I received the incredible opportunity to visit the Netherlands. This urbanist pilgrimage taught me so much about urban planning, and how wrongly my country is doing it. Here are three counterintuitive things I learned about how to take back a country from the cars.
